strengths: Addresses a genuine and important practical bottleneck for diffusion LLMs (lack of KV cache and quality degradation under parallel decoding), with a training-free solution that is immediately deployable to existing open-source models.

Extensive empirical evaluation across two model families (LLaDA, Dream), an improved variant (LLaDA-1.5), and a multimodal variant (LLaDA-V), spanning four text benchmarks and two multimodal benchmarks, demonstrating broad applicability.

Strong and consistent speedups (up to 27.6x end-to-end, 8-11x combined on standard settings) with generally minimal (1-2 point) accuracy degradation, and in some cases even slight accuracy improvement.

Provides a theoretical analysis (Theorem 1 with full proof) characterizing when parallel decoding via marginals is equivalent to sequential decoding under a high-confidence condition, giving some principled grounding to the proposed threshold/factor decoding strategies beyond pure heuristics.

Good supporting analyses: KV-activation cosine similarity heatmaps justify the caching approximation, and thorough ablations (cache block size, prefix vs. dual cache, prefill/generation length effects, threshold vs. factor strategy, batch-size scaling vs. AR models) give a fairly complete picture of the method's behavior.
Qualitative case studies and an honest limitations discussion (e.g., diffusion LLMs remain compute-bound and don't scale as well with batch size as AR models) add credibility and transparency.
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat incremental: block-wise KV caching for diffusion LLMs is conceptually close to prior block-diffusion approaches, and confidence-based selective unmasking is a natural extension of existing top-k confidence remasking strategies already used in LLaDA; the main contribution is largely a careful combination/engineering of known ideas rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

Theorem 1 relies on an idealized, well-defined joint PMF assumption that the paper itself admits MDMs may not strictly satisfy (Remark 1), and the practical threshold (0.9) is not tightly derived from the bound, weakening the claimed 'theoretical justification' for the specific hyperparameters used.

No comparison against alternative diffusion-LLM acceleration or caching methods (e.g., other approximate attention/caching schemes, other parallel-decoding heuristics) beyond the paper's own ablations, making it hard to assess relative merits versus concurrent/prior acceleration techniques.

The approximation error introduced by KV cache reuse (especially DualCache, which caches masked suffix tokens whose true keys/values will change) is only justified qualitatively via similarity heatmaps on a single model, without deeper theoretical or systematic error analysis across models/tasks.

Accuracy is not uniformly preserved (e.g., some benchmarks show >1-2 point drops such as MBPP at length 512, or fluctuations on HumanEval), and results are reported as single runs without variance/error bars despite the stochastic nature of confidence-based decoding.

Section C.5 reveals that diffusion LLMs (even with the proposed caching) still scale worse than AR baselines at larger batch sizes, an important practical limitation that is somewhat underexplored/underemphasized relative to the paper's strong headline speedup claims.
Minor presentation issues (typos, e.g., 'hgiher' in the introduction) suggest incomplete proofreading.
